usage: 종류 = category; the first thing every form and officer asks
받다 is the natural verb of receiving, never 가지다
만료(滿了)되다 = run out fully; the word printed at immigration
신청하다 = to apply; what you do before you 받다
examples: 저는 학생 비자예요.
I'm on a student visa.
Simplest form: just name the purpose + 비자 + 예요, no D-codes in daily speech.
제 비자는 다음 달에 만료돼요.
My visa expires next month.
만료돼요 is the spoken contraction of 만료되어요; note 비자가/는, not 비자를, with 만료되다.
무슨 비자로 들어오셨어요?
What visa did you enter the country on?
An officer's question; the particle 로 marks the visa as the means of entry, and 들어오다 = come in.
nuance: 비자 is the everyday English loanword (from 'visa'); the native-style Sino-Korean term 사증(査證, literally 'inspect-certify') exists on official paperwork but nobody says it aloud. The nearest thing learners confuse it with is 여권 (passport): a 여권 is the booklet that proves who you are, while a 비자 is the permission stamped or linked to it that lets you enter and stay — you can hold a 여권 with no valid 비자. In conversation Koreans name the purpose and attach 비자 (워홀 비자, 결혼 비자, 학생 비자) instead of the official D-2/F-6 codes. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb: English 'have a visa' tempts you into 비자를 가지다, but Korean uses 비자를 받다 (receive) to obtain one and 비자가 있다 (exist) to possess one; pair it with officials' words 만료되다 (expire) and 연장하다 (extend).

Confusing 비자 (the entry/stay permission) with 여권 (the passport booklet); an officer asking about your 비자 does not want to see only your 여권 photo page.
Calling it 사증 in conversation because a dictionary lists it; 사증 is written-only — say 비자 when you speak.

usage: your official visa category; the term officers use
기간 = duration; how long you may legally remain
불법(不法) = unlawful; the status to avoid at all costs
pairs with 연장; the most common foreigner errand
examples: 체류 자격이 어떻게 되세요?
What is your residence status?
The set polite formula 어떻게 되세요? softens a request for official personal info.
체류 기간을 6개월 연장했어요.
I extended my period of stay by six months.
기간 + 연장하다 is the standard pairing; 6개월 marks the added length.
기간이 지나면 불법 체류가 되니까 꼭 연장하세요.
If the period passes it becomes overstaying, so be sure to extend.
되다 = become; this shows 체류 inside the real consequence learners fear.
nuance: 체류(滯留) is built from 滯 'stagnate/linger' + 留 'remain', so it literally paints someone staying put in a place — and it is pure bureaucratic register, almost never used alone but locked into fixed compounds (체류 자격, 체류 기간, 체류 연장). The everyday verb learners reach for is 머무르다 'to stay/linger', and that is exactly the dividing line: you 머무르다 at a hotel or a friend's house for a night, but your legal right to be in the country is your 체류 — an abstract immigration status, not a physical act of lodging. You will meet this word constantly on HiKorea (하이코리아) and at the 출입국 office, and the most important phrase is 체류 자격, your visa type. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the verb 'stay': you cannot say 호텔에서 체류했어요 for 'I stayed at a hotel' (use 묵었어요/머물렀어요); 체류 belongs to paperwork, not to where you slept.

usage: 신청 = applying; the core counter pairing
the reason most foreigners ever use this word
the 하다-verb you say at the desk or type online
same word works for housing leases and jobs
examples: 비자 연장하고 싶어요.
I'd like to extend my visa.
Simplest counter line: noun + 연장하다 + 고 싶어요, no extra words needed.
계약을 1년 더 연장했어요.
I extended the contract by one more year.
더 = 'more'; shows 연장 reaching beyond visas into housing leases.
연장 신청이 거절될 수도 있어서 서류를 잘 준비하세요.
The extension application could be rejected, so prepare your documents well.
거절되다 = be rejected; -ㄹ 수도 있다 hedges the real risk.
nuance: 연장(延長) means 延 'prolong' + 長 'long', so it literally stretches the length of something time-bound — visas, lease contracts (계약 연장), library loans, deadlines. The word it is constantly confused with is 갱신(更新) 'renewal': 연장 adds more time onto the same existing thing, whereas 갱신 issues a fresh new one to replace the old (you 갱신 a passport or membership card, you 연장 the period you may stay). For immigration it is almost always 체류 연장 or 비자 연장, and the working verb is 연장하다, what you say at the counter. The English-speaker pitfall is the bare imperative: copying 'extend it, please' as 연장 주세요 sounds broken because 연장 is a noun, not the thing being handed over — say 연장하고 싶어요 ('I want to extend') or 연장 신청하러 왔어요 ('I came to apply for an extension') instead.

usage: 하다 is the verb; you 'do' the report
기한 = due date; within 14 days of moving
마치다 = complete; what you confirm afterward
to go file a move-in report
examples: 이사하면 전입신고를 해야 돼요.
When you move, you have to file a move-in report.
Core rule in one line; -으면 = 'when/if', -아야 되다 = obligation.
전입신고하러 주민센터에 가는 길이에요.
I'm on my way to the community center to file a move-in report.
가는 길이에요 = 'on the way to'; 주민센터 is the place you go.
전입신고를 해야 확정일자를 받아서 보증금을 지킬 수 있어요.
Only after filing the move-in report can you get a fixed-date stamp and protect your deposit.
-아야 = 'only if/after'; ties 전입신고 to protecting your 보증금.
nuance: 전입신고(轉入申告) is a four-character compound: 轉 'turn/shift' + 入 'enter' + 申 'state' + 告 'report', literally 'report of shifting-in', i.e. declaring to your new district office that you have moved IN. Learners blur it with its mirror-image 전출(轉出) 'moving OUT': in practice you almost never file 전출 yourself — registering your new address with 전입신고 automatically cancels the old one, so 전입신고 is the action that matters. It is a legal must-do at the local 주민센터 within 14 days of moving, and for renters it unlocks 확정일자, the date-stamp that legally protects your deposit, which is why locals treat it as urgent rather than optional. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: this is a 신고 (a formal report you 하다), so you say 전입신고를 하다, never 전입신고를 쓰다 or 만들다 as if writing a document — and missing the 14-day 기한 can bring a fine.

Treating it as optional paperwork; it is legally required within 14 days and missing the 기한 can incur a fine, plus you lose deposit protection without it.

usage: the full name; 등본 is everyone's short form
떼다 is THE colloquial verb for official documents
발급 = the formal act behind 떼다
examples: 등본 한 통만 떼 주세요.
Please issue me just one copy of the extract.
Counter line: 한 통만 = 'just one copy'; staff 떼 주다 it for you.
회사에서 등본을 제출하래요.
My company says to submit a resident extract.
제출하래요 = contracted 제출하라고 해요, '(they) tell me to submit'.
등본은 정부24에서 인터넷으로 떼서 출력하면 돼요.
You can pull the extract online at Gov24 and just print it.
-에서 marks the site; 떼서 출력하다 = issue then print, the modern way.
nuance: 등본(謄本) means 謄 'transcribe/copy out' + 本 'original document', i.e. a certified transcript of an original register; in daily life it is short for 주민등록등본, the household sheet listing everyone registered at your address, demanded constantly for jobs, bank accounts, and contracts. The document people mix it up with is 초본(抄本) 'an excerpt copy' (抄 'extract'): the 등본 shows the whole household at one address, while the 초본 traces one individual's personal history including past addresses — offices specify which one they need, so the difference is not cosmetic. The signature English-speaker pitfall is the verb: you do not 받다 ('receive') a 등본, you 떼다 it — 떼다 literally means 'to peel/detach off', the idiomatic word for pulling an official copy, as in 등본 떼러 가요 ('I'm going to get an extract'). Foreigners get the parallel 외국인등록사실증명, but everyone still says 등본 colloquially.

Confusing 등본 (the whole household at an address) with 초본 (one person's address history); offices ask for one specifically and the wrong one gets rejected.
Forgetting the counter 통; you ask for 등본 한 통, not 등본 하나, when requesting copies at the counter or kiosk.

usage: full name; people shorten it to 출입국
the office handling visas and registration
the older official name still seen on signs
examples: 외국인등록은 출입국에서 해요.
Foreigner registration is done at the immigration office.
-에서 marks where the action happens; 외국인등록 is the process itself.
출입국 예약은 하이코리아에서 미리 하세요.
Book your immigration appointment in advance on HiKorea.
미리 = 'beforehand'; you almost always need a reservation first.
공항 출입국 심사대 앞에서 여권을 미리 꺼내 두세요.
Have your passport out before the airport passport-control desk.
심사대 = inspection desk; 꺼내 두다 = take out and keep ready.
nuance: 출입국(出入國) literally stacks 出 'exit' + 入 'enter' + 國 'country', so the word itself means 'leaving-and-entering the country' and serves as the everyday short name for the 출입국·외국인청/사무소, where foreigners handle visas, registration, and extensions. The trap is that learners flatten it with its one-directional halves 출국 (出國, departing) and 입국 (入國, arriving): 출입국 is the round-trip concept and, by extension, the office/process, whereas 출국 and 입국 each point one way only — you do 출국 심사 when leaving and 입국 심사 when arriving, but the building is the 출입국. At the airport the same root appears in 출입국 심사 (passport control). The practical English-speaker pitfall is assuming you can simply walk in like a U.S. DMV: most 출입국 civil tasks require a 하이코리아 (HiKorea) online reservation first, so 예약하다 before 가다.

usage: for bank cards, ID cards, transit cards
use 받다 when you are the recipient
what you say to the staff member
examples: 카드를 잃어버려서 재발급받아야 해요.
I lost my card, so I have to get it reissued.
잃어버리다 = lose; 재발급받다 keeps you as the receiver of the action.
체크카드 재발급은 며칠 걸려요?
How many days does debit-card reissuance take?
며칠 걸려요? = 'how many days does it take', the natural timing question.
외국인등록증을 도난당해서 재발급 신청서를 작성하고 있어요.
My residence card was stolen, so I'm filling out the reissuance application.
도난당하다 = have something stolen; shows the realistic reason for 재발급.
nuance: 재발급(再發給) prefixes 再 'again' onto 발급 '발(發) issue + 급(給) grant', so it literally means 'issuing-and-granting again' — what you request when a document is lost, stolen, or damaged and a replacement must be produced: bank cards, ID, residence card, transit card. The word it must be told apart from is 갱신(更新) 'renewal': 재발급 replaces a copy that is gone or broken (the underlying right is unchanged), while 갱신 is for something whose validity has simply expired and needs updating — so a stolen card is 재발급 but an expired one is 갱신. The recurring English-speaker pitfall is voice/perspective: the citizen says 재발급받다 ('have it reissued', receiver) or asks staff 재발급해 주세요 ('please reissue it'), but learners over-apply 재발급하다 to themselves, which actually describes the office that does the issuing, not the person receiving it.

Saying 재발급하다 about yourself; the citizen 재발급받다 (receives), while the office 재발급하다 / 재발급해 주다 (issues).
Pairing it as 재발급을 사다 because you pay a fee; you 재발급받다 and separately 수수료를 내다 — the fee is paid, the document is not bought.

usage: to fill out an application form
작성하다 is the correct office verb, not 쓰다
제출하다 = hand in; casual equivalent is 내다
양식 = the blank form layout you fill in
부 = the counter for copies of documents
examples: 여기 신청서 작성해 주세요.
Please fill out the application form here.
The single most common counter instruction; 작성하다 = fill out formally.
신청서에 서명하는 걸 잊지 마세요.
Don't forget to sign the application form.
-에 marks where you sign; 잊지 마세요 = 'don't forget'.
작성한 신청서는 저쪽 창구에 내시면 돼요.
You can submit the completed form at that window over there.
내다 = the everyday word for 제출하다; 창구 = service window.
nuance: 신청서(申請書) is 申 'state' + 請 'request' + 書 'document', literally a 'document stating a request', i.e. any fill-in application form, from visa extensions to library cards. The piece learners confuse it with is plain 신청 (申請), the act of applying: 신청 is what you DO (online or verbally), while the 신청서 is the physical/PDF sheet you complete — '신청을 했어요' means you applied, '신청서를 작성했어요' means you filled out the form. The natural collocation verb is 작성하다 ('compose/fill out'), which sounds far more correct in offices than the literal 쓰다 'write'. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 쓰다 reflex from 'write a form', plus the handing-in step: staff tell you 내세요 or 제출하세요 to submit it, so the full life cycle is 신청서를 작성하다 → 제출하다, and you will hear 신청서 작성해 주세요 at virtually every Korean counter.

The natural collocation verb is 작성하다 ('compose/fill out'), which sounds far more correct in offices than the literal 쓰다 'write'. The piece learners confuse it with is plain 신청 (申請), the act of applying: 신청 is what you DO (online or verbally), while the 신청서 is the physical/PDF sheet you complete — '신청을 했어요' means you applied, '신청서를 작성했어요' means you filled out the form.
신청서(申請書) is 申 'state' + 請 'request' + 書 'document', literally a 'document stating a request'.
The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 쓰다 reflex from 'write a form', plus the handing-in step: staff tell you 내세요 or 제출하세요 to submit it.

mistakes: Using 쓰다 ('write') instead of 작성하다 ('fill out') for completing a form; 작성하다 is the standard, more correct office verb.
Confusing 신청서 (the form you complete) with 신청 (the act of applying) — 신청을 하다 = apply, 신청서를 작성하다 = fill out the form.
Counting forms with 개; documents take the counter 부, so it is 신청서 한 부, not 신청서 한 개.

usage: the 하다-verb you do at the counter
처(處) = place; where you hand things in
the tracking number you get after applying
for the intake to be processed
passive; your paperwork is now in the system
examples: 서류 접수는 몇 시까지예요?
Until what time can documents be submitted?
몇 시까지 = 'until what time'; 접수 here is the intake window.
접수가 완료되면 문자로 알려 드려요.
Once the intake is complete, we'll notify you by text.
완료되다 = be completed; 알려 드리다 is the humble 'inform you'.
병원에 도착하면 먼저 접수처에서 접수하고 기다리세요.
When you reach the hospital, first register at the intake desk and wait.
Shows the real hospital flow: 접수하다 first, then wait for your number.
nuance: 접수(接受) joins 接 'receive/connect' + 受 'accept', literally 'receiving and accepting', the bureaucratic word for an office taking in and logging your application or documents — at a clinic or government window you 접수하다 first, then wait for your number, and 접수가 됐어요 means your paperwork is officially in the system. The deceptive lookalike for English ears is 영수증 (領收證) 'a payment receipt': both translate as 'receipt', but 접수 is the intake/registration of your case, whereas 영수증 is the proof-of-payment slip you keep — totally different documents despite the shared gloss. The directional English-speaker pitfall mirrors 발급/재발급: you, the applicant, 접수하다 (submit) or 접수시키다, while the office 접수받다 (accepts it); reversing them makes you sound like the clerk. Register is mildly formal but heard everywhere from hospitals to immigration desks.

Treating 접수 as merely 'reception' for greeting visitors; in offices it specifically means logging your case into the system, with a 접수 번호 issued.

usage: to get issued / to be issued (to me)
use this when you are the recipient
the request you make to staff
즉시 = on the spot; e.g. instant cards at a kiosk
passive; 'it gets issued' on its own
examples: 외국인등록증은 며칠 후에 발급돼요.
The residence card is issued a few days later.
발급되다 = the passive 'gets issued'; 며칠 후에 = 'a few days later'.
증명서를 한 통 발급받고 싶어요.
I'd like to be issued one copy of the certificate.
발급받다 keeps you as the receiver; 한 통 uses the document counter.
여기서는 임시 카드를 즉시 발급해 드려요.
Here we issue a temporary card on the spot.
발급해 드리다 is the humble form staff use toward you; 임시 = temporary.
nuance: 발급(發給) is 發 'send out/issue' + 給 'grant/supply', literally 'issuing and supplying', the official act of producing and handing over a card or certificate — it covers IDs, residence cards, and every kind of 증명서. It sits in a tight family learners scramble: 발급 is issuing a brand-new document, 재발급 is reissuing one that was lost or damaged, and 갱신 is renewing one that expired — three different counter requests, not synonyms. The persistent English-speaker pitfall is voice: like a verb that flips with perspective, the citizen says 발급받다 ('have it issued', receiver) or asks 발급해 주세요, the office says 발급하다 / 발급해 드리다, and the document itself 발급되다 / 발급됩니다 (passive). Saying 제가 발급했어요 to mean 'I got one issued' wrongly casts you as the issuing office. The word is plastered on every Korean kiosk and counter (즉시 발급, 무인 발급).

usage: 내다 is the verb for paying a charge
for a fee to be incurred
for a fee to be added on
붙다 = to be tacked on (e.g. transfers)
examples: 수수료가 얼마예요?
How much is the fee?
The simplest counter question; 얼마예요? = 'how much is it'.
송금할 때 수수료가 좀 붙어요.
A fee gets tacked on when you transfer money.
붙다 = be added; 좀 softens it to 'a bit'.
이 신청은 수수료가 따로 없어서 무료예요.
There's no separate fee for this application, so it's free.
따로 없다 = 'there isn't a separate one'; ties to 무료.
nuance: 수수료(手數料) is a wonderfully literal compound — 手 'hand' + 數 'number/effort' + 料 'fee', i.e. a fee for the hand-labor/effort of processing — the catch-all word for an administrative or service charge on bank transfers, card reissuance, document issuance, and booking platforms. It must be separated from two neighbors: 요금(料金) is a usage charge for consuming a service (fares, electricity, phone bills), and 세금(稅金) is tax paid to the government — so a transfer's processing cost is 수수료, your monthly data plan is 요금, and VAT is 세금. Collocationally you 수수료를 내다 (pay it) and it 붙다 / 들다 (gets added / is incurred). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb 'buy': 'I bought... a fee' makes no sense, so never 수수료를 사다 — fees are paid (내다) or incurred (들다), and many counters proudly advertise 수수료 무료.

mistakes: Confusing 수수료 (a processing/service charge) with 요금 (a usage charge like fares and bills) or 세금 (tax to the government).
Saying 수수료를 사다 because in English you 'pay for' things; you 수수료를 내다 (pay) or it 든다 (is incurred), never 'buy' it.
Assuming any fee is 수수료; a fine is 벌금 and a fare is 요금 — 수수료 is specifically for processing a service or document.

usage: what staff ask you to do
확인 = checking; announced before a task
examples: 신분증 좀 보여 주시겠어요?
Could you show me your ID, please?
보여 주시겠어요? is a very polite request; 좀 softens it further.
외국인은 외국인등록증이 신분증이에요.
For foreigners, the residence card serves as the ID.
Explains the foreigner equivalent; A이/가 B예요 = 'A is B'.
신분증을 안 가져와서 술을 못 샀어요.
I couldn't buy alcohol because I didn't bring my ID.
안 가져오다 = 'didn't bring'; a real age-check situation.
nuance: 신분증(身分證) is 身 'body/person' + 分 'standing/status' + 證 'certificate', literally a 'certificate of one's personal standing', and it is the umbrella term for any government photo ID — 주민등록증, 운전면허증, 여권, or for residents the 외국인등록증. The contrast learners need is that 신분증 is the category, not a specific card: a 주민등록증 (the resident registration card Koreans carry) is one kind of 신분증, but so is your passport, so an officer asking for 신분증 is not demanding a Korean card specifically. You will be asked 신분증 있으세요? at banks, pharmacies, offices, and when buying alcohol or cigarettes, and many counter tasks (접수, 발급) require 신분증 확인 first, so always carry one. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: assuming 신분증 means only the Korean 주민등록증 (your 외국인등록증 or 여권 counts), and confusing the near-homophone 신청서 (application form) with 신분증 (ID) — they sound alike to beginners but are entirely different objects.
